---
title: "Beginnings & endings"
author: "Tim Gorringe"
date: "2023-05-10"
categories: ["Physics"]
format: html

In physics we've different ways of conceptualizing how things works. This is
helpful to physicists both in solving physics problems and in deepening physics
understanding. It's similar to psychology in which there's different ways of
conceptualizing how humans act. This is helpful to psychologists both in solving
human problems and in deepening human understanding.

For electricity, we'll discover that supplementing the concept of fields with
notions of flux is akin to adding a few wrenches to the screwdrivers in your
toolbox. It make some jobs easier, shorter, and much less frustrating.

Visualize a washbasin. And imagine a stream of water from the faucet, across the
floor of the basin, into the drain. Below I've sketched the stream of water
using 'stream lines'. The line directions indicate the direction of flow. Water
streams from the faucet, across the basin, and into the drain. The line
densities indicate the strength of the stream. Water gushes from the relatively
narrow faucet outlet and gushes into the relatively narrow drain inlet. By
comparison the water idles over the wide bottom of the wash basin between the
faucet and the drain.

There's something important you intuitively know about the flow of water from
faucet to drain. The quantity of water that's leaving the faucet, crossing the
basin, and entering the drain, are exactly the same. Water isn't created or
destroyed en-route from faucet to drain. The quantity of water per unit of time
in kilograms per second or cubic-meters per second is conserved.

In our sketch the lines are drawn to emerge from the faucet and exit into the
drain. If I count the number of lines that exit the faucet, cross the floor of
the basin, and enter the drain, they're exactly the same. The continuous lines
from the faucet across the basin to the drain indicate the conservation of the
water. In the sketch we can think of the faucet as a water 'source', from which
water enters our washbasin-world, and we can think of the drain as a water
'sink', into which water exits out washbasin-world.

The stream lines in our sketch of the water in a washbasin are very similar to
the field lines in a sketch of the electric field of a charge arrangement.
Positive charge act as sources (faucets) of field lines and negative charge act
as drains (sinks) of field lines. In regions of empty space between electric
charge the field lines are continuous, i.e., no beginnings and no ends.

Of course there's nothing that is moving in electric fields that's analogous to
the motion of running water. But still the idea of flow is applicable to both
electric fields and running water. The electric field and running water both
have direction at every point in space. The electric field and running water
both have magnitude at every point in space. Both electric fields and running
water flow - whether abstract or concrete.

To quantify the notions of charges as sources and sinks of field and flow of
fields through space we introduce a quantity called flux. Note that flux and
field are related. Qualitatively, the density of field lines at a given point
indicates the electric field at that point. And qualitatively, the number of
field lines through a given surface indicates the electric flux through that
surface.

In order to quantitatively define flux let's consider a flat surface in a
uniform field. The flux ϕ of the field through the surface is the product of the
cross-sectional area A of the surface and the normal component E⟂ of the field,
ϕ = E⟂A.

Gauss' law states that the net electric flux through a closed surface is
proportional to the net electric charge inside the closed surface. A closed
surface is a particular surface with a definite inside and a definite outside.
If you're inside a closed surface you'll have to cross the surface to be outside
the closed surface. If you're outside a closed surface you'll have to cross it
wall to get inside the closed surface. We write Gauss' law ϕ = q / ε~o~ where
ε~o~'s a constant that called the electric permittivity of free space.

Imagine a charged blob q and a closed backpack. If the blob is inside the
backpack the next flux through the backpack is q / ε~o~. It doesn't matter if
the blob is packed at the top or the bottom of the backpack the net flux through
the backpack is always q / ε~o~. In this case every field from the charge in the
backpack passes out of the backpack. If the blob is outside the backpack the
next flux through the backpack is zero. It doesn't matter if the blob is close
to or far from the backpack the net flux through the backpack is always zero. In
this case any field line that passes into the backpack must also pass out of the
backpack.

Charlie only knows Coulomb's law whereas Chloe also knows Gauss' law. Their
physics teacher asks Charlie and Chloe to calculate the electric field of a
large, planar, charged slab with a charge per unit area σ \[C/m^2^\]. Chris
worked the entire weekend on mathematically cleaving the slab into tiny pieces
and superimposing the inverse-square Coulomb fields of all pieces. Chloe spent a
few minutes thinking about the electric flux and reasoned the field on either
side of the slab is σ / 2ε~o~. This way of thinking of charges as sources and
sinks of flux is extraordinarily helpful in understanding fields of simple
geometries such as slabs, cylinders and spheres.
